evaluation.positioning_hook: A sleep-deprived teen’s disappearance pulls a Guatemalan-American family into a murder investigation where grief, queer identity, and folk demonology collide in one Atlanta house.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediate: a missing teen, a family in crisis, and a horror overlay rooted in recognizable emotional stakes. The audience is real but somewhat targeted toward elevated-genre buyers and viewers who like culturally specific, prestige-leaning scares.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast through Shelly’s breakdown, the buried-in-soil image, and the later investigation that reframes the disappearance. The script makes the central mystery legible early and keeps adding layers rather than muddying the core question.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Shelly is a vivid, volatile center, and María, Mike, Ana, and Alex all have distinct emotional functions in the family system. The supporting cast around the café and GBI adds texture without flattening the lead dynamics.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldness comes from fusing Atlanta procedural realism with Guatemalan spiritual imagery and queer family trauma. The final surreal sequence, with saints, El Sombrerón, and the family members embodied as icons, is a confident stylistic swing.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The investigation scenes move cleanly from family concern to police skepticism to the reveal of Manuel’s identity and death. The middle is more procedural than propulsive, but the soil mystery and the stalker truck keep the engine active.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script feels fresh because the supernatural and the procedural are not decorative; they are braided into the family’s cultural memory and the case facts. The buried-soil image and the El Sombrerón imagery give the premise a memorable signature.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Buford Highway, the café, the GBI room, and the family home all feel socially specific and story-generating. The multilingual household, the immigrant/refugee history, and the neighborhood ecosystem create a world with real friction and lived-in detail.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually specific: grounded family drama, procedural skepticism, and then full surreal horror. The script knows exactly when to stay naturalistic and when to go operatic, which gives it a distinct identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are deeper layers around inherited trauma, queer erasure, spiritual belief, and family guilt that the script only partially opens up here. The mythology and the family altar imagery suggest a much larger emotional and cultural backstory.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The family table scenes generate strong recurring energy, and the café ensemble adds a second relational system with its own tensions. Mike/María, Ana/Shelly, and the GBI pair all have usable friction that can keep scenes alive.

lead_characters.name: Shelly Cano
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 19, Mexican American/Guatemalan American, queer/trans-adjacent identity context implied through the Manuel relationship and family dynamics.
lead_characters.hook: Shelly is the script’s emotional fuse: sleep-deprived, obsessive, and increasingly unmoored as she tries to locate Manuel and make sense of the stalker she believes is following her. She reads as a young woman whose pain is both psychological and possibly supernatural, which gives the role volatility, vulnerability, and mystery.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is showcase territory in the vein of Toni Collette in Hereditary or Jessie Buckley in Men — a role that asks for raw breakdowns, physical deterioration, and the ability to hold the audience inside a destabilizing interior state.

lead_characters.name: María Ixcol De Garcia
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 70s, K'iche' Guatemalan refugee, Spanish-speaking elder.
lead_characters.hook: María is the family’s spiritual anchor and its sharpest truth-teller, carrying refugee memory, Catholic ritual, and indigenous belief in the same breath. She can be funny, blunt, and devastating in the same scene, and her grief history gives the story its deepest emotional authority.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the authority and specificity of Rita Moreno in One Day at a Time or Adriana Barraza in Babel — a lived-in elder with humor, pain, and moral force.

lead_characters.name: Miguel Cano
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 50s, Mexican American, landscaping business owner.
lead_characters.hook: Mike is the practical family patriarch trying to keep work, home, and crisis from collapsing at once. He’s warm, exhausted, and emotionally porous, which makes him a strong counterweight to both the police and the supernatural material.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, emotionally layered father role that lets an actor play competence under strain, similar to Pedro Pascal in The Last of Us or Michael Peña in A Million Miles Away.

lead_characters.name: Ana Cano
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 50s, pediatric nurse, bilingual Spanish/English speaker.
lead_characters.hook: Ana is the family’s caretaker and mediator, trying to keep Shelly alive while also managing her mother’s fear and her husband’s exhaustion. She’s compassionate but not passive, and the role lives in the painful space between denial and alarm.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This gives an actor the kind of emotionally precise mother role seen in America Ferrera in Barbie or Patricia Velásquez in The Curse of La Llorona — steady, wounded, and forced into crisis management.

lead_characters.name: Alejandro Cano
lead_characters.hook: Alex is the younger brother with the easiest laugh in the house, but he’s also the one who cracks under the family’s pressure in the later scenes. He gives the script a younger, more contemporary point of entry and a real emotional release valve.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong teen supporting role in the lane of Noah Jupe in A Quiet Place or Jack Dylan Grazer in It — funny, observant, then suddenly heartbreaking.

lead_characters.name: Sue Kim
lead_characters.demographics: Female, adult, special agent, Korean American.
lead_characters.hook: Kim is the cool, strategic investigator who sees through the local cops’ complacency and keeps pushing the case toward the truth. Her deadpan control gives the procedural material bite and makes her a memorable authority figure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp, controlled investigator role that plays like Carrie Coon in The Leftovers or Jodie Comer in The End We Start From — intelligence, restraint, and a dry edge.

lead_characters.name: Omar Gaines
lead_characters.hook: Gaines is the warmer half of the investigative duo, a listener who can still push hard when the facts demand it. He gives the audience an entry point into the case and a human counterbalance to Kim’s colder precision.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a solid, scene-steadying investigator role in the tradition of Mahershala Ali’s quieter procedural work or Sterling K. Brown’s grounded authority — empathy with backbone.

lead_characters.name: Valentina Rojas
lead_characters.hook: Valentina is the café boss with warmth, speed, and a protective instinct toward her staff and Shelly. She’s a social hub character who can pivot from hospitality to suspicion in a beat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of vibrant supporting role that lets an actor do charisma and authority at once, like Stephanie Beatriz in Brooklyn Nine-Nine or Adria Arjona in Good Omens.

lead_characters.name: Gloria Martinez
lead_characters.hook: Gloria is the grieving sibling who finally clarifies Manuel’s life and the family pressure he was hiding from. She’s emotionally direct, and her scenes supply the story’s most painful human context.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a clean, emotionally loaded supporting turn in the vein of Auli’i Cravalho in The Power or Ariana DeBose in West Side Story — grief, intelligence, and moral clarity.

lead_characters.name: Padre Esteban Morales Ramirez
lead_characters.hook: Padre Esteban is the spiritual intermediary who seems gentle on the surface but becomes part of the film’s uncanny pressure system. He’s a useful ambiguity engine because he can read as pastoral, ominous, or both.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor quiet authority and menace, similar to Ralph Ineson in The Witch or Mark Margolis in Better Call Saul — presence more than volume.

casting_characteristics: Spanish/English code-switching required for several roles
Latine family ensemble with age-specific elder casting

notable_requirements: family home with basement apartment, altar, garage, and office
GBI conference room and office locations
night exterior on Cheshire Bridge Road

technical.vfx_details: Surreal horror sequence requires stylized transformations, lighting shifts, and possibly compositing for the El Sombrerón/saint embodiment imagery; otherwise mostly practical.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical bathtub soil fill, body burial imagery, camera glitch/static effects, and stylized dream/horror transitions.

rights_flags.detail: "Estilo Bélico" by Lil Jhay is specifically named in a flashback.
"Marcha Número Cuatro" by The San Lucas Band is specifically named in the surreal sequence.
"Amor Dificil" by Los Flamas is specifically named over the ending.
"Exorcismo Documentado" (2012, dir. Rodrigo Estrada Alday) is specifically referenced on the TV.
GrayKey is specifically named as the phone-unlock tool.
Canon EOS Rebel is specifically named in the field-search sequence.
Happy Cake is specifically named as a breakfast brand.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: premium streaming or prestige theatrical genre
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: prestige genre launch with festival-to-streaming or specialty theatrical path.

budget.note: Contemporary interiors keep the base spend contained, but the stylized horror finale, night exterior on Cheshire Bridge, and multiple named music cues add cost pressure beyond a simple contained drama.

casting.note: The family ensemble needs bilingual performers with cultural specificity, and Manuel’s trans identity plus the Guatemalan/K'iche' context narrows the search for authenticity.

development.note: The script’s tonal handoff from procedural family drama into full surreal horror is a real selling point, but it also creates a buyer conversation about how much supernatural expression the feature should carry.

comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the family-grief-to-occult-horror escalation and the sense that inherited trauma is the real monster.

comp_set.title: The Night House
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the grief-driven mystery structure and the way the lead’s emotional unraveling becomes the engine of the scares.

comp_set.title: A Ghost Story
comp_set.why_it_comps: Not in tone, but in the patient use of loss, memory, and domestic space as the emotional architecture.

comp_set.title: The Blackcoat's Daughter
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the eerie, restrained-to-operatic horror shift and the sense of a young woman being swallowed by something older than herself.

comp_set.title: His House
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the immigrant-family trauma, supernatural pressure, and culturally specific haunting as a metaphor for survival.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult genre viewers who want elevated horror with family emotion, cultural specificity, and a mystery that pays off in a memorable final act.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skew, slightly female-leaning, urban/coastal and streamer-native, with strong appeal to Latinx and prestige-horror audiences.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary Atlanta locations, a mostly interior family/café/procedural footprint, and one stylized horror set-piece keep this in indie-feature territory.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where emotional family drama is the entry point and the horror payoff is the differentiator. The Buford Highway specificity and the Guatemalan spiritual imagery give it a buyer-facing identity beyond generic possession or missing-person material.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the story resolves around Shelly, Manuel, and the family’s crisis, with no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond this case.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Buford Highway feels like a lived-in world
strengths.what_it_means: That specificity gives the project a commercial moat: it doesn’t read like generic suburban horror, it reads like a place with its own social rules and visual identity. Buyers looking for elevated genre with a strong sense of place will see immediate differentiation.
strengths.evidence: The street-sign opener, the landscaping business, the café on Cheshire Bridge, and the family’s multilingual home all root the story in one Atlanta ecosystem.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family table scenes carry real heat
strengths.what_it_means: The script has a built-in emotional engine that can sell beyond horror fans because the family conflict is legible and painful on its own. That makes it attractive to actors and to buyers who want genre with awards-adjacent emotional credibility.
strengths.evidence: Shelly’s breakdown at breakfast, María’s blunt grief, Alex’s cracking voice, and Ana/Mike trying to hold the room together.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The cultural mythology is not decorative
strengths.what_it_means: The Guatemalan spiritual material gives the horror a proprietary angle that can’t be swapped out without losing the script’s identity. That kind of specificity is valuable in a crowded elevated-horror market because it creates both marketing hooks and critical distinction.
strengths.evidence: Tzizimite, El Sombrerón, the altar, the saints, and the final surreal procession sequence.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The procedural spine keeps the mystery legible
strengths.what_it_means: The GBI investigation gives the project a clean commercial engine, which helps buyers understand the story even before the horror fully blooms. That structure broadens the lane from pure art-horror into a more accessible mystery-thriller hybrid.
strengths.evidence: The conference-room breakdown of the burner phone, the soil mismatch, the CCTV glitch, and the reclassification of Manuel’s death.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Shelly is a strong actor magnet
strengths.what_it_means: The lead role offers a rare combination of emotional breakdown, physical deterioration, and surreal horror imagery, which is exactly the kind of part that can attract a serious young actor. That matters because a compelling lead performance can materially lift the package and the buyer conversation.
strengths.evidence: Shelly’s sleepless unraveling, her frantic search for Manuel, and the bathtub burial image.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige-horror package with a real identity: culturally specific, emotionally loaded, and visually memorable. The script gives buyers a contained contemporary production with a strong lead role, a clear mystery spine, and a final-act horror swing that feels ownable rather than generic.

items.area: The feature is built from episode grammar.
items.detail: The script is labeled as a feature, but the structure reads like a serialized episode: cold open, investigation blocks, flashback reveals, and a final tag. That is not a fatal flaw, but it is the first thing a buyer will notice because it affects how the material is packaged and paced as a standalone film.

items.area: The horror turn arrives late and hard.
items.detail: Most of the runtime is family drama and procedural inquiry before the surreal horror sequence fully takes over. That makes the tonal payoff strong, but it also means the buyer has to trust the script’s promise of genre escalation before the feature’s identity is fully on display.

items.area: The named music and TV references need clearing.
items.detail: "Estilo Bélico," "Marcha Número Cuatro," "Amor Dificil," and the referenced film "Exorcismo Documentado" are all specific clearance items. None of them are deal-killers, but they do create a real legal and budget pass before greenlight.

items.area: The lead role depends on a very specific performance lane.
items.detail: Shelly has to play panic, dissociation, grief, and possible supernatural possession without losing audience sympathy. That is a strong showcase, but it narrows casting to actors who can sustain a volatile, physically expressive lead role for the full feature.

items.area: The final surreal sequence is a buyer test.
items.detail: The El Sombrerón / saint-embodiment passage is the script’s boldest signature, but it also pushes the film into a highly stylized register that some buyers will love and others will see as a tonal commitment. It is the kind of sequence that defines the package, for better or worse.

issues.headline: The main friction is structural: this reads like a serialized episode that then detonates into a feature-length horror finale. Add the clearance work on the named music and the need for a very specific lead performance, and the project becomes a strong but conditional buy.
